19856-a-study-of-pueblo-architecture-tus:
Victor Mindeleff studied pueblo architecture for the Bureau of Ethnology. His study covers Tusayan and Cibola, the Hopi and Zuni country. It appeared in the Bureau's Eighth Annual Report. Pueblo remains scatter over thousands of square miles of arid Southwest. The region runs from the Rio Pecos to the Colorado River. It stretches from central Utah beyond the national border.

Mindeleff measured cliff dwellings, terraced towns, and great houses. His plans and drawings set a standard for the field. Living pueblos helped him read the abandoned ones. The report joined archaeology to living Native practice. It remains a foundation document of Southwestern studies. Few government reports have lasted so well.
20078-merely-mary-ann:
Merely Mary Ann is a novel set in Baker's Terrace, a small South London side street. The builder Baker gave the street its name, the book explains. Houses there look much alike, like a batch of cheap loaves. Only black doorsteps, save on Sundays, break the sameness of the row.

Mary Ann's story grows from that plain, cramped world of lodgings. Small streets can hold big hopes, slights, and loves all the same. The book finds drama in servants, clerks, and quiet rooms. Readers get London life at street level, told with humor and a warm eye.
21473-paddy-finn:
Terence O'Finnahan, called Paddy Finn, stands before his ancestral castle on the Shannon in W. H. G. Kingston's Paddy Finn. The major greets him with the top of the morning from a bedroom window. Whisky, warm water, and Irish talk set the scene at Ballinahone.

The tale tracks Paddy through his years at sea as a midshipman. Event follows event, fast and furious, in one of Kingston's longest stories. Kingston's deep store of sea knowledge shows on every page. Judges have ranked the book among his best, and it suits readers who love a full, bustling naval yarn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelmann:
Adelmann, Brescia's eleventh-century bishop of unknown parentage and origin, was educated at Chartres's famous school in France, founded by Fulbert, and ranked among his prized pupils. Fellow student Berengarius later received two letters from him. The second, incomplete, letter is a valuable statement of church teaching on the Blessed Sacrament.

The Benedictine editors of the Histoire litteraire de la France rank it among the period's finest literary writings. It breathes tender love for Berengarius, the friend of his youth. Calvin, by contrast, called Adelmann crude, unskilled, and a sophist. Adelmann apparently became Brescia's bishop in 1050 and took an active part in the church reform movement, especially against simony and concubinage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-kau:
Alexander Kaufmann was a German poet and folklorist, born at Bonn in May 1817 and dead at Wertheim in May 1893. He came of a well-known Bonn patrician family and was related to the painters Andreas and Karl Müller. At Bonn he studied law, languages, and history. In 1844 he became teacher to Prince Karl von Löwenstein-Wertheim-Rosenberg. The prince made him keeper of the archives at Wertheim in 1850, a post he held until his death.

Kaufmann published Poems in 1852, Main Legends in 1853, and Under the Vines in 1871. His research for Karl Simrock's Rhine legends and his own Main legends are highly valued. With the poet Georg Friedrich Daumer he compiled a book of myths, sagas, and legends. He worked critically on Caesarius of Heisterbach, translating his wonderful stories between 1888 and 1891. His life of the Belgian Dominican Thomas of Cantimpré appeared after his death in 1899.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antony-kohlma:
Alsatian Jesuit Antony Kohlmann was born at Kaiserberg in 1771 and dead in Rome in 1836. He ranks among the luminaries of the restored Society of Jesus and its leading members in America, where he passed nearly a quarter century. Driven by the French Revolution to Switzerland, he finished theology at Fribourg and was ordained. Then he joined the Fathers of the Sacred Heart in 1796 and laboured as a military chaplain in Austria and Italy. He directed a seminary at Dillingen, then worked in Berlin and Amsterdam.

When Pope Pius VII recognized the Jesuits in Russia in 1801, Kohlmann joined the Society and entered the novitiate at Dunaburg in 1803. A year later a call for workers in the United States sent him to Georgetown, where he became assistant to the superior. The entry follows an educator and missionary whose career crossed revolution, exile, and the rebuilding of Jesuit life on two continents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-jungm:
Bernard Jungmann, a dogmatic theologian and church historian, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Münster in Westphalia in 1833, he died at Louvain in 1895. Raised in an intensely Catholic family, he studied at the German College in Rome and the Gregorian College, taking a doctorate in philosophy in 1854.

Teaching at Louvain became his life's work, with textbooks on dogma and church history that trained generations of priests. Two brothers also served the Church, one as a Jesuit and one as a missionary in America. The entry presents a clear, systematic teacher whose books outlived his classroom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-altma:
Blessed Altmann, Bishop of Passau and papal legate, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Paderborn near the start of the eleventh century, he headed the school there and served as chaplain at Henry III's court before becoming bishop. Friend of Gregory VII and Anselm, he stood conspicuous in the age's great contests.

As bishop he was famed for care of the poor, vigour in reforming lax monasteries, founding new ones, and splendour in worship, with Henry IV himself giving toward his works. The Bollandists note that his successive posts make it impossible to call him a Benedictine monk. The entry presents a reforming bishop of the Gregorian age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bruenn:
Bruenn, suffragan diocese of Olmutz in southwestern Moravia, covers 3,825 square miles with about 1,051,654 people, over a million of them Catholic. Its creation came from Empress Maria Theresa, who found Olmutz too vast to rule alone. In 1773 she opened talks with Clement XIV, and Pius VI's bull of 5 December 1777 raised Olmutz to an archbishopric and erected Bruenn.

The old provostship of Saints Peter and Paul, standing since 1296, became the cathedral chapter, and its provost church became the cathedral. Matthias Franz von Chorinsky, the mitred provost, served as first bishop, followed by Lachenbauer, Schrattenbach, Stuffler, Gindl, Schaffgotsche, Nottig, Bauer, and Huyn. The diocese counts 429 parishes, 545 mission churches, and 751 secular clergy in parish work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bruno-franz-l:
Bruno Franz Leopold Liebermann, Alsatian theologian, shaped the Catholic revival at Mainz through the clergy he trained. Born at Molsheim on 12 October 1759, he studied theology at Strasburg from 1776 to 1780, taught at Molsheim, and was ordained priest on 14 June 1783. He preached at Strasburg cathedral in 1784 and served as pastor at Ernolsheim from 1787.

Driven across the Rhine in the Revolution, he ran the exiled Strasburg seminary at All Saints in the Black Forest, teaching dogma and canon law. He worked in secret at Ernolsheim from 1795 to 1801 and survived eight months in a Paris prison in 1804 on a groundless royalist suspicion. He then led the new Mainz seminary from 1805. His pupils included future bishops Rass, Weis, and Geissel. He declined Metz in 1823, served as Strasburg vicar-general, and died at Strasburg in 1844.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clementine-de:
Clementine Deymann, born at Klein-Stavern in Oldenburg on 24 June 1844 and died at Phoenix, Arizona, on 4 December 1896, reached America in 1863. There he took the habit of Saint Francis and the name Clementine on 8 December 1867. He was ordained priest at Saint Louis, Missouri, on 19 May 1872.

He taught at Teutopolis College until July 1879. Then he served at Joliet as prison chaplain and spiritual director of the School Sisters. In August 1880 he became superior and pastor at Joliet's German parish. In July 1882 he took a like position at Chillicothe. In 1885 and 1891 he was elected definitor of his Franciscan province. In 1886 he became superior of the Watsonville boys' orphanage. On 22 July 1896 he became first commissary of the new Pacific Coast Franciscan commissariat. He died shortly after and was buried at Santa Barbara. In spare time he translated useful works and wrote manuals for the Third Order and for Saint Francis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-maginn:
Edward Maginn was coadjutor Bishop of Derry and a force in the rebirth of the Ulster Church, born at Fintona in 1802 and dead at Derry in 1849. Son of a farmer, he was taught by his uncle and at Buncrana, then entered the Irish College in Paris in 1818. Ordained at Derry in 1825, he won fame as a preacher at Movilla and fought public debates against Protestant proselytising.

As parish priest of Fahan from 1829 he opposed secret societies and pressed the government to shield tenants from harsh magistrates. He backed Catholic Emancipation, stood with O'Connell for Repeal, and fought to keep schools under clerical care while rejecting the Queen's Colleges. Consecrated coadjutor in 1846, he died of typhus three days after falling ill in January 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-hei:
Friedrich Windischmann, an orientalist and exegete born at Aschaffenburg in 1811, ranked among the greatest Eastern scholars of his day. Son of the philosopher Karl Joseph Windischmann, he studied philosophy, classics, and Sanskrit at Bonn, then theology at Bonn and Munich, plus Armenian with the Mechitarists at Venice. Ordained in 1836, he rose to vicar-general of Munich by 1846.

Windischmann knew Armenian and Old Persian well, along with several Sanskrit dialects, and he defended papal rights boldly against state meddling. His books range from a study of Vedanta thought to essays on the soma rite, Aryan origins, the goddess Anahita, and Mithra. A posthumous volume of Zoroastrian studies and a fine commentary on Galatians round out his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georg-hartman:
Georg Hartmann, a mechanician and physicist born in Bavaria in 1489, built the instruments of his age at Nuremberg. After studying theology and mathematics, perhaps under Glareanus and Melanchthon, and traveling in Italy, he settled at Nuremberg in 1518 as a maker of globes, astrolabes, sundials, and like devices. His craft served scholars, sailors, and churchmen alike.

Hartmann's name lives chiefly through the magnetic dip, the tilt of a magnetized needle on its axis, which he is credited with finding in 1544. The angle varies by place, a fact his careful balancing revealed. Later he served as vicar of Saint Sebaldus church in Nuremberg, publishing papers on astrological subjects until his death there in April 1564.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heilsbronn:
Franconia's Heilsbronn, a former Cistercian house in the Eichstätt diocese, was founded in 1133 by St. Otto of Bamberg with monks from Ebrach under Abbot Rapatho. Rich gifts from the Abenberg dukes and their heirs, the Nuremberg burgraves, filled it, and its church holds the tombs of most of those burgraves and of Brandenburg's electors.

Flourishing until the Reformation, it turned under Abbot John Schopper, who founded a monastic school in 1530, and his successor Sebastian Wagner, who married and resigned in 1543, toward Protestantism. Catholic worship restored in 1549 was only a show. The last nominally Catholic abbot ruled to 1578, five Protestant abbots followed, and Heilsbronn lost abbey status in 1631, its library now at Erlangen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-biderma:
Poet and theologian James Bidermann, born at Ebingen, Germany, in 1578 and dead at Rome on 20 August 1639, stood out from an early age in many branches of learning. His reputation ran so high that Matthew Rader, a Dillingen professor, celebrated him in a Latin poem as another Aquinas, Aristotle, Cicero, and Virgil.

After usual training, he entered the Society of Jesus at Landsberg in 1594. He taught rhetoric at Munich from 1606 to 1615. He then spent eight years teaching philosophy and theology at Dillingen. Called to Rome in 1624, he served as theologian and censor of books until death. Besides dramas, epigrams, and biographical sketches, he wrote many books on philosophy and theology. Best known are Theses Theologicae of 1620, Sponsalia of 1621, and other theological works. The entry presents a Jesuit polymath of baroque Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-baltha:
Johann Balthasar Neumann, a German architect born at Eger in 1687 and dead at Würzburg in 1753. He stands as master of rococo and one of the eighteenth century's greatest and most fruitful builders. He came to Würzburg as a cannon founder, served chiefly with the French army, and travelled to perfect his craft across southern Germany and the Rhine.

In Prince-Bishop Schönborn's service from 1719, Neumann laid the Würzburg palace cornerstone in 1720. The vast rectangle, 544 by 169 feet, holds five courts and three pillared gates, with throne room, state rooms, and court chapel outshining the rest in sumptuous rococo. French judges de Cotte and Boffrand later claimed the authorship themselves, having judged his plans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-herman:
Johann Hermann, a Belgian Catholic theologian born at Maaseik in 1783 and dead at Engis in 1853, studied theology at Rome and taught at Fribourg College from 1809 to 1816. There he wrote his Hermeneutica, published in 1818 after he moved to Liège seminary as Scripture and dogma professor.

Charged with heterodoxy, Hermann was removed in 1823 and made pastor at Engis, then against superiors' will took Louvain's anthropology and metaphysics chair until revolution closed the college in 1830. Retiring to Engis, he wrote a three-volume Netherlands history from a Protestant standpoint. Abroad he is known chiefly for his Sacred Hermeneutics, in nineteen editions by 1897 with a French version from 1828.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-joachi:
Johann Joachim Winckelmann, archaeologist and historian of ancient art, was born at Stendal in 1717 and murdered at Trieste in 1768. After a wandering youth of eager classical study on scant means, he settled in Saxony in 1748 near Dresden's treasures, working in a count's library.

Painter Oeser led Winckelmann to judge art critically and spurred his Thoughts on Imitating Greek Works of 1755, coining noble simplicity and calm greatness for Greek statues. Turning Catholic in 1754, he won a royal pension for Rome late in 1755, studying Capitol, Vatican, and villa collections. He stood as archaeology's greatest authority, a rank he kept through a life cut short by murder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-clynn:
John Clynn was an Irish Franciscan annalist whose Annals of Ireland close amid the Black Death. Born about 1300, he became guardian of the Franciscan convent at Carrick in 1336 and later lived at Kilkenny, where he probably died in 1349. Ware credits him with works on English kings and Franciscan superiors, neither published.

His fame rests on his Annals from the birth of Christ to 1349, meagre at first but vivid from 1315, when he writes of what he saw himself. Anglo-Irish himself, he speaks harshly of native chiefs yet condemns Anglo-Irish lords for their impatience of restraint, contempt for Dublin, and oppression of the poor. The plague of 1348 to 1349 is the subject of his unforgettable account. Amid the dead and dying, he set down his pen, wondering whether any son of Adam would be spared. His copyist adds that there the author seems to have died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-fenn:
John Fenn was an English priest and scholar who preserved the records of Catholic persecution under Elizabeth. Born at Montacute near Wells, eldest brother of the martyr James Fenn, he was a chorister at Wells, scholar at Winchester, and fellow of New College, Oxford, in 1552. Deprived of his headmastership and fellowship for refusing the supremacy oath, he went to Rome, was ordained about 1566, and settled at Louvain for forty years.

He contributed to the 1583 Concertatio, the collection of persecution accounts that formed the groundwork of Bridgewater's larger work of 1588, and gathered treatises written for Syon's Brigittine nuns. As first chaplain of St. Monica's Priory at Louvain from 1609 until blindness in 1611, he kept working, translating Fisher on the penitential psalms, the Trent catechism, and lives of saints, until his death in 1615.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-jungman:
Josef Jungmann was a German Jesuit priest and teacher at Innsbruck who lived from 1830 to 1885. Born at Münster in Westphalia, he entered the German College in Rome in 1850, was ordained in 1855, and joined the Society of Jesus. Even before finishing his novitiate, he was chosen in 1858 to hold the chair of elocution, the art of public speaking, in Innsbruck's restored theology faculty.

His books dealt largely with devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the dangers of light fiction reading. His work on the theory of sacred preaching ran to two volumes and went through several editions. Students remembered him for high principles and a steady character that shaped his teaching, his friendships, and his daily religious life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-salzma:
Joseph Salzmann was an Austrian pioneer priest who founded Wisconsin's Salesianum seminary. Born at Münzbach in 1819 and ordained in 1842, he worked in his home diocese until Bishop Henni of Milwaukee appealed for priests in 1847. Salzmann sailed that October and soon became pastor of St. Mary's in Milwaukee, fighting bitter abuse from German free-thinkers.

Seeing the shortage of priests, he raised funds state by state and opened St. Francis Seminary on 29 January 1856 with twenty-five students. Hundreds of priests and twenty-three bishops later called it home. He also founded America's first Catholic normal school, Pio Nono College, and the American branch of the St. Cecilia Society for church music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-echter:
Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn was the Prince-Bishop of Würzburg who restored Catholicism there. Born in 1545 at Mespelbrunn Castle, he studied at Mainz, Louvain, Douai, Paris, and Rome, became canon of Würzburg in 1567, and was named prince-bishop in 1573 at twenty-eight, before ordination. His diocese was debt-ridden and nearly all Protestant.

Echter backed the Jesuits, founded Würzburg University in 1582 as a model Counter-Reformation school, and used it to train priests and officials. He banished Lutheran preachers, required Catholic officials and teachers, and taught non-Catholics with care and some threat. Within three years about one hundred thousand returned to the Church. He died at Würzburg in 1617.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-joseph-h:
Karl Joseph Hieronymus Windischmann was a philosopher born at Mainz in 1775 and dead at Bonn in 1839. He studied philosophy, natural science, and medicine at Würzburg until 1796, then practiced medicine at Mainz from 1797. In 1801 the Elector summoned him to Aschaffenburg as court physician. Two years later he became professor of philosophy and history there, and in 1818 professor of philosophy and medicine at Bonn.

He fought Hermesianism at Bonn and gave Rome opinions on it in 1834 and 1835. His early philosophy, in Ideen zur Physik of 1805, was a pantheistic mysticism under Schelling, which he hoped to unite with Christianity. Gradually he reached a positive Christian philosophy. His chief work planned a Christian philosophy of history, though its four volumes of 1827 to 1834 treated only China and Japan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leopold-acker: This 1913 reference piece on Ackermann — a German writer of note. John Joseph A'Becket lists his works. Little is known of his career. The nineteenth century was his period. The learned press knew his pen. His 1890 works are famed. His 1890 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leopold-kaufm: A 1913 entry on Kaufmann — the Bonn mayor. Karl Hoeber notes his famous city. His rule built the Rhenish town. The burghers bless the prudent name. The nineteenth century knew his sway. His 1898 death is famed. His 1898 Bonn is famed. His 1898 Rhenish city is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monk-of-heils: The Monk of Heilsbronn was a 14th-century German Cistercian whose mystical writings circulated widely in manuscript. This entry covers his works, his spirituality, and his influence. An anonymous voice of medieval mysticism, whose works were treasured by later contemplatives and copied in many manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-bachmann: This biographical entry profiles Paul Bachmann, a German churchman of the early modern era, tracing his career and his service as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's German gallery, preserved among its early modern churchmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-laymann: Paul Laymann was the Jesuit moralist whose Moral Theology guided confessors through the Thirty Years' War. This entry covers his career, his works, and his authority. The casuist of the war years: his wise judgments steadied many troubled consciences in wartime.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodor-schwa: Schwann was the father of the cell. This long entry examines his 1839, his microscope, and his fame. The physiologist of the animal tissue: his famed 1839 crowned Berlin in the academy of the Müller in the very old hall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-augu: Mann was the historian of the Low Countries. This entry traces his Brussels, his works, and his exile. The English priest of the Austrian Netherlands: his many works crowned Brussels in the 1700s of the academy in the old city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-will: Achtermann was the sculptor of Rome. This entry traces his 1800s, his marble, and his Pietà. The German artist of the sacred stone: his marble Pietà crowned Rome in the 1850s of the Thorvaldsen in the truly very old studio.
doe-osti-2587510-aerodynamic-characteriz: 3D-scanned wind blades got their aero characterization, and this DOE report covers experimental and computational methods. The pages detail the findings. The wind engineers get their data. The blades were 3D scanned. The methods were experimental. The engineers got data.
doe-osti-3002166-the-oak-ridge-national-: ORNL's Seaborg Institute got its 2025 highlights, and this DOE text celebrates the year's work. The pages detail the achievements. The lab folks get their roundup. The institute was Glenn T. Seaborg. The roundup was lab. The achievements were detailed. The year was 2025.
doe-osti-3018003-large-load-planning-sit: Large loads got siting-planned, and this DOE text covers interconnection. The pages detail the findings. The grid folks get their data. The planning was load. The data were grid. The interconnection was siting. The loads were large. The text was DOE's.
doe-osti-3365880-conference-support-for-: CU*IP got conference-supported, and this DOE text covers UCONN support. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their data. The support was conference. The data were researcher. The UCONN were IP. The researchers were data. The support were conference.
doe-osti-3740041-characterization-of-pos: Baffle bolts got annealed-characterized, and this DOE text covers post-irradiation grips. The pages detail the characterization findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The X-ray was in-situ high energy. The data were nuclear. The grip were design.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIWarrenCommis:
An FBI report numbered ZBC-1 records an interview on December 11, 1963 at St. David's Hospital in Austin. The patient was Governor John Connally of Texas, wounded in the Dallas shooting that killed President Kennedy. From his hospital bed, Connally recounted his experience of the shots.

Connally was the closest surviving witness to the president at the moment of the shooting. What he remembered about the shots, their order, and his own wounds became key evidence. The report fixes that memory nineteen days after the event, in the words the Bureau wrote down.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KinneyEdwardChr:
Harold Weisberg spent decades challenging the official account of the Kennedy assassination, and this April 25 letter shows his method. His subject is the Navy's refusal to say who its Surgeon General was. The letter also takes up the Sibert-O'Neill report and the testimony of Dr. Pierre Finck, who was involved in the autopsy.

FBI agents James Sibert and Francis O'Neill filed their report on the autopsy of President Kennedy. Finck's testimony about that examination became a point of dispute among researchers. Weisberg argues that official silence on such small, checkable points hides basic facts. The letter presses an agency on details and builds a case from its answers.
grillparzer-der-arme-spielmann:
A poor street fiddler in Vienna plays badly, loves hopelessly, and carries a whole life of sorrow in his music. Grillparzer's Der arme Spielmann, given here in German, is his most famous story. A festival-goer narrates, slowly coming to understand the mocked old musician he first pitied from a distance.

The fiddler's tale unfolds in layers: a lost inheritance, a patient love, a flood, and music as the vessel of it all. Unrecognized genius and quiet sanctity meet in one humble figure. Critics rank the novella among the great short works of world literature. Its portrait of failure transfigured by devotion has moved readers for generations. Few Austrian stories are loved more tenderly.
hartmann-iwein-benecke-lachmann:
Hartmann von Aue retold the tale of Yvain in German as Iwein, and the Benecke and Lachmann edition keeps that text in print. The version here, revised by Wolff, runs the full 8,165 verses. Iwein is a knight of Arthur's court who wins a wife and a land.

Iwein breaks his word to his lady and loses her love and his wits at once. Mad in the woods, he is healed and must climb back by deeds of service. A lion he saves fights at his side the rest of the way. The poem stands as a peak of medieval German courtly romance.
hofmannsthal-jedermann:
A rich man named Everyman receives a summons from Death and finds his companions unwilling to follow. Hugo von Hofmannsthal's Jedermann, from 1911 and given here in German, retells the medieval morality play for modern audiences. Performed every summer at the Salzburg Festival since 1920, it has become Austria's most beloved play.

Medieval in form and modern in feeling, the drama asks what a life is worth when the accounts are finally called. Money, friends, and good deeds each answer the summons in turn. Hofmannsthal's verse gives the old allegory fresh music and ache. Open-air performances before Salzburg cathedral made the play a national ritual. The German text lets readers hear why it holds the stage so firmly.
nasa-tm-19700026410-an-analysis-of-parac:
Noel C. Willis Jr. and Edward T. Chimenti of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this working paper on June 21, 1967. It analyzes how much heat a parachute takes in a crewed launch abort. In an abort, the capsule may pass near the fireball of its own failing rocket before its parachutes fully open.

The main parachute gets a full description first, then a heating study split by flight stage. Stages run from line stretch through the opening steps to steady descent under canopy. A separate method covers the smaller drogue parachutes that fly earlier in the sequence. An estimate of the fireball itself anchors the heat figures used throughout the analysis.
the-castle-inn: Stanley J. Weyman, author of A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe, wrote this novel, dated 1898 and illustrated by Walter Appleton Clark. Only the title page and a full list of twenty-eight chapters are present here, with titles that name a tutor and his pupils, a pursuit, an empty post-chaise, and a rough awakening.Beyond the front matter, nothing is present to describe.
the-flying-inn:
Gilbert K. Chesterton wrote The Flying Inn as a comic novel, printed at New York in 1914. A list of his past books at the front runs from The Napoleon of Notting Hill to The Innocence of Father Brown.

Chesterton sets his tale in an England where a strict league seeks to stamp out drink and close the inns. One inn sign, saved and carried on a cart, turns into a flag of revolt. Poems, songs, and wild debates fill the road as the inn moves from place to place. The book defends warmth, song, and local custom against cold schemes to rule men's lives.
the-lady-of-lynn: Sir Walter Besant published this novel with Dodd, Mead and Company in 1901, under copyright of 1900. He had written All Sorts and Conditions of Men. A frontispiece caption preserves one line of dialogue, a man's grateful reply to a lord. Only the title pages, copyright page, and contents heading are present here. The story itself does not appear. Lynn, the Norfolk port of the title, waits beyond the pages shown. Its lady must be met there too.
the-mystery-of-31-new-inn:
R. Austin Freeman's detective novel The Mystery of 31 New Inn opens with its narrator recalling his association with John Thorndyke. Few men living within hearing of Big Ben, he writes, can match his wealth of strange adventures. Many are already on record, yet the most astonishing remains untold: the case that began his permanent partnership with Thorndyke.

A contents list of sixteen chapters maps the case ahead. A mysterious patient comes first, then Thorndyke devising a scheme, Jeffrey Blackmore's will, and a cuneiform inscription. A track chart, a house of mystery, and a hunter hunted follow, before Thorndyke lays and explodes his mine, in the chapter titles' mining metaphor. Freeman is billed as author of The Red Thumb Mark and The Eye of Osiris.
the-red-inn:
Honore de Balzac's tale, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley and dedicated to the Marquis de Custine, begins at a Paris banker's dinner table. His guest Hermann, head of a Nuremberg house met only through business letters, proves stout, learned, fond of pipes, and devoted to champagne and Johannisburger alike.

Balzac lingers over German appetite and good nature as Hermann takes a conscientious farewell to great French cooking. Other guests, merchants and agreeable women, complete a cordial evening. A story told at such a table will carry the weight of confession, and readers settle in for the German's tale within the tale.
the-repair-of-casa-grande-ruin-arizona-i: Cosmos Mindeleff reports on repairing the Casa Grande ruin. The ruin stands in Arizona, and the work fell in 1891. Contents cover a description of the ruins first. Their condition that year follows. Plans for the repair come next. The execution of the work and the land reservation follow. Specimens found in the diggings close the report proper. Exhibits add the contract and the specifications. Bids and official reports appear there too. Only the title page and contents list are present here. The repair account itself does not appear.
the-second-william-penn:
W. H. Ryus wrote The Second William Penn, dated 1913. Its subtitle promises a true account of incidents along the old Santa Fe Trail in the sixties. Colonel Milton Moore supplied a preface. Moore says he knew the author intimately. Ryus did not draw on imagination for his incidents, Moore insists. He adhered strictly to the truth.

Moore praises Ryus's knowledge of Indian character and traits. His tact in trading and treating with Indians sustained friendly relations, Moore writes. That success was one of the wonders of the West. It won Little Billy of the Stage Coach his title, the Second William Penn. In the early sixties the trail crossed unexplored territory, Moore recalls. Freight caravans drawn by oxen traveled it. So did lumbering Concord stage coaches drawn by five mules.
